To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
evaluators systematically rate research proposals more negatively when the proposals are close to the evaluator’s own research and when the proposals are highly novel.

evaluators systematically rate research proposals more negatively if they are closer to the evaluator’s own area of expertise, and if the proposals are more novel, and that this is consistent with a bounded rationality explanation, and inconsistent with an explanation that intellectual distance is just a source of noise in evaluations, or an explanation that evaluators have private interests in evaluating proposals.

(1) the intellectual distance between the knowledge embodied by a research proposal and an evaluator’s expertise systematically relates to evaluation scores and (2) this relationship is consistent with evaluators being biased against proposals that are close to their own expertise and highly novel.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the allocation of resources in scientific knowledge creation.
how organizations allocate resources to new ideas.
the evaluation of frontier science.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our findings support the view that the intellectual distance of the evaluator from the proposal has a systematic effect on the score that he/she assigns to it.
the intellectual distance between a proposal and an evaluator is negatively related to the evaluation scores of the proposal.
the distance of the proposal to the evaluator's expertise has a negative effect on the evaluation of the project.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evaluation of scientific research proposals is biased.

the evaluation of research proposals by peers in science systematically depends on the “distance” between the knowledge that is embodied in the proposal and the knowledge that is possessed by the evaluator.

the more distant the knowledge embodied in a project is from the knowledge of the evaluators, the more likely the project is to get funded, but only if the evaluators have a good understanding of the field.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evaluation of scientific proposals is biased in ways that are predictable, systematic, and potentially amenable to intervention.
the evaluation of frontier projects by experts in a field is not a straightforward process.
intellectual distance between evaluators and proposals systematically affects the evaluation of scientific research proposals.
